questions.q: How many membrane-spanning helices characterize the GPCR family shown?
questions.explanation: The slide identifies GPCRs as receptors containing seven transmembrane helices.

questions.q: What produces the amplification step highlighted in the GPCR diagram?
options: One receptor activates multiple G proteins
One G protein creates multiple receptors
questions.explanation: An active ligand-bound receptor can successively activate multiple G proteins.

questions.q: Which event directly ends signaling by an individual G-alpha subunit?
questions.explanation: G-alpha's GTPase activity hydrolyzes bound GTP to GDP, returning the subunit to its inactive state.

questions.q: Which enzyme is activated by G-alpha in the pathway described on the slide?
questions.explanation: Activated G-alpha binds and activates adenylyl cyclase in the illustrated pathway.

questions.q: What happens after G-alpha hydrolyzes its bound GTP?
questions.explanation: GDP-bound G-alpha reassociates with beta-gamma, reforming the inactive trimeric G protein.

questions.q: In the Aplysia images, which color represents the highest intracellular cAMP concentration?
questions.explanation: The slide's color scale identifies blue as low, yellow as intermediate, and red as high cAMP.

questions.q: In this signaling example, serotonin is classified as which messenger?
questions.explanation: Serotonin binds the extracellular receptor and is therefore the first messenger; cAMP is the second messenger.

questions.q: Which kinase is directly activated by cAMP in the illustrated liver-cell cascade?
questions.explanation: cAMP activates protein kinase A in the glucagon/epinephrine cascade.

questions.q: What is the immediate metabolic purpose of activating glycogen phosphorylase in this pathway?
questions.explanation: Glycogen phosphorylase promotes glycogen breakdown, helping mobilize glucose.

questions.q: Why are G proteins and arrestins mutually exclusive at an activated GPCR?
options: They bind the same cytoplasmic receptor cavity
questions.explanation: Both engage the same inter-helical cavity on the receptor's cytoplasmic side, so binding of one prevents binding of the other.

questions.q: Which receptor-modifying enzyme acts before arrestin binds?
questions.explanation: A GPCR kinase, or GRK, first phosphorylates the active receptor.

questions.q: What happens to the overall volume of a cell and its nucleus during apoptosis?
options: The cell increases while the nucleus shrinks
questions.explanation: Shrinkage of both the cell and nucleus is listed as a characteristic feature of apoptosis.

questions.q: Which cell-surface change is characteristic of apoptosis on this slide?
questions.explanation: Apoptotic cells lose adhesion and form blebs at the cell surface.

questions.q: Which event appears first in the illustrated apoptotic sequence?
questions.explanation: The diagram begins with chromatin condensation, followed by blebbing, nuclear collapse, and apoptotic-body formation.

questions.q: What is the final labeled morphological product of the sequence?
questions.explanation: The dying cell fragments into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies.

questions.q: Where are engulfed apoptotic bodies degraded inside macrophages?
questions.explanation: Macrophages phagocytose apoptotic bodies and degrade them within phagolysosomes.

questions.q: Which property of apoptotic bodies helps prevent inflammation?
options: They retain an intact enclosing plasma membrane
They release ATP into surrounding tissue
questions.explanation: Membrane enclosure prevents cellular contents from spilling into the surrounding tissue.

questions.q: Which death receptor is named in the extrinsic apoptosis pathway?
questions.explanation: The slide begins the pathway with TNF binding to TNFR1.

questions.q: Which pair consists of adaptor proteins recruited in the TNFR1 complex?
questions.explanation: Activated TNFR1 recruits the cytoplasmic adaptors TRADD and FADD.

questions.q: Which set contains only anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members listed on the slide?
questions.explanation: BCL-2, BCL-XL, and MCL-1 are all listed as anti-apoptotic proteins.

questions.q: What cellular event is caused by BAX and BAK oligomerization?
questions.explanation: BAX and BAK form pores that permeabilize the mitochondrial outer membrane, producing MOMP.

questions.q: From which mitochondrial compartment is cytochrome c released during intrinsic apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c resides in the intermembrane space before MOMP releases it into the cytosol.

questions.q: Which initiator caspase is activated by the cytochrome c–Apaf-1 complex?
questions.explanation: The intrinsic pathway recruits and activates procaspase-9.

questions.q: Where is phosphatidylserine normally located in a healthy cell?
options: Outer leaflet of the plasma membrane
Cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane
questions.explanation: In healthy cells, phosphatidylserine is maintained on the cytoplasmic, inner leaflet.

questions.q: What biological signal does exposed phosphatidylserine provide to macrophages?
questions.explanation: Externalized phosphatidylserine marks the apoptotic cell for engulfment.

questions.q: Which treatment is used on the slide to induce apoptosis?
questions.explanation: The treated cells were exposed to staurosporine to induce apoptosis.

questions.q: In untreated cells, cytochrome c fluorescence is expected to appear in which pattern?
questions.explanation: Before mitochondrial permeabilization, cytochrome c remains localized to mitochondria and appears punctate.

questions.q: Which phases together constitute interphase?
questions.explanation: Interphase consists of G1, S, and G2.

questions.q: What structure performs the equipartition of chromosomes during mitosis?
questions.explanation: The mitotic spindle organizes and separates chromosomes into the two daughter cells.

questions.q: Which fluorescent stain is identified as a DNA stain on this slide?
questions.explanation: The slide explicitly states that propidium iodide is used to stain DNA.

questions.q: Which listed purpose of mitosis is especially important in skin and gut lining?
questions.explanation: Mitosis replaces damaged, worn-out, or dead cells in rapidly renewed tissues such as skin and gut lining.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of the cell cycle is spent in interphase according to the slide?
questions.explanation: The slide labels interphase as approximately 90% of the cell cycle.

questions.q: Which phase is described as a quiescent state outside active cycling?
questions.explanation: Cells that temporarily or permanently stop dividing enter G0.

questions.q: What is the DNA state of each decondensed chromosome in G1?
questions.explanation: Before S phase, each G1 chromosome consists of one linear double-stranded DNA molecule.

questions.q: During which phase are sister chromatids generated?
questions.explanation: Chromosome replication in S phase creates sister chromatids.

questions.q: At which mitotic stage do spindle microtubules gain access to chromosomes and attach to kinetochores?
questions.explanation: The slide describes kinetochore attachment after nuclear-envelope breakdown in prometaphase.

questions.q: At which stage are chromosomes aligned at the spindle midplane?
questions.explanation: Chromosome alignment at the spindle midplane defines metaphase.

questions.q: Why does transcription decrease as chromosomes compact in prophase?
questions.explanation: The slide states that transcription shuts down partly because compaction displaces transcription factors.

questions.q: Toward where do the centrioles move as the mitotic spindle forms?
questions.explanation: The centrioles move toward opposite cell poles while spindle microtubules extend between them.

questions.q: Approximately how many different polypeptides are stated to assemble into the human kinetochore?
questions.explanation: The slide states that approximately 100 different polypeptides assemble into kinetochore protein complexes.

questions.q: Which motor protein is named as helping carry chromosomes along spindle microtubules?
questions.explanation: Dynein is named as a kinetochore-associated motor that moves chromosomes on the spindle.

questions.q: During which stage are sister chromatids pulled toward opposite poles?
questions.explanation: Separation and poleward movement of sister chromatids occur in anaphase.

questions.q: What is the name of the process that physically pinches one cell into two daughter cells?
questions.explanation: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and completes physical cell separation.

questions.q: Which material was transferred from a maturing Xenopus oocyte into an immature oocyte?
questions.explanation: Cytoplasm from a maturing oocyte was injected into an immature recipient.

questions.q: What response in the recipient oocyte indicated induced maturation?
questions.explanation: The injected recipient underwent germinal-vesicle breakdown and prematurely entered meiosis.

questions.q: Which cyclin-CDK complex is most associated with the G1/S transition in the diagram?
questions.explanation: Cyclin E–CDK2 activity peaks around the G1/S transition.

questions.q: Which cyclin is shown rising through S and G2 before declining in mitosis?
questions.explanation: The plotted Cyclin A activity spans S phase and G2.

questions.q: In which phosphorylation state is pRb active as an E2F inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Hypophosphorylated pRb binds and inactivates E2F transcription factors.

questions.q: Loss of RB1 function also increases risk of which malignancy named on the slide?
questions.explanation: The slide specifically names osteosarcoma and soft-tissue sarcomas as additional risks.

questions.q: Which progenitor gives rise to B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes, and natural killer cells in the diagram?
questions.explanation: B, T, and natural killer cells branch from the common lymphoid progenitor.

questions.q: Which mature blood cell is produced from a megakaryocyte?
questions.explanation: The diagram shows thrombocytes/platelets arising from megakaryocytes.

questions.q: Which specialized function is assigned to red blood cells on the slide?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells are given as the example specialized for O2 transportation.

questions.q: What is differentiation?
options: Replacement of a cell's entire genome
Permanent arrest of every stem cell
questions.explanation: Differentiation is the process by which unspecialized cells acquire specialized morphology and function.

questions.q: Which term describes the range of cell types that a cell can potentially become?
questions.explanation: Developmental potential, or potency, is the range of cell types a cell can become.

questions.q: How does developmental potential generally change as development proceeds?
options: It remains identical in all cells
questions.explanation: Cell fates become progressively restricted, so developmental potential decreases.

questions.q: Which potency class has the broadest developmental potential?
questions.explanation: Totipotent cells can generate all cell types required for an organism.

questions.q: Which potency class is restricted to producing one specific cell type?
questions.explanation: A unipotent cell produces only its own specific cell type.

questions.q: What does clonality mean in the lineage diagram?
options: Cells originate from one founder cell
Cells arise from multiple unrelated founders
questions.explanation: A clone is a group of descendant cells derived from one founder.

questions.q: What triggers expansion of the selected lymphocyte clone in the diagram?
questions.explanation: Antigen selects the matching lymphocyte clone, which then proliferates.

questions.q: In the potency pyramid, in which direction does differentiation increase?
questions.explanation: The diagram shows broad totipotency at the apex and increasingly differentiated cell types toward the base.

questions.q: How does potency change as cells move toward differentiated cell types?
questions.explanation: Developmental potency narrows as differentiation proceeds.

questions.q: What is the direct molecular cause of different behavior in differentiated cells according to the slide?
options: Different subsets of genes are expressed
questions.explanation: Differential gene expression gives different cell types different protein complements.

questions.q: What do the contrasting colors in the two heat maps primarily represent?
questions.explanation: Heat-map color differences represent relative expression levels of gene sets in the compared progenitors.

questions.q: What is the fluid-filled cavity in a blastocyst called?
questions.explanation: The hollow cavity shown inside the blastocyst is the blastocoel.

questions.q: Which cell layer surrounds the mammalian blastocyst in the diagram?
questions.explanation: The outer cell layer of the blastocyst is labeled trophoblast.

questions.q: Which three primary germ layers are established during mammalian gastrulation?
questions.explanation: Gastrulation establishes ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

questions.q: Which germ layer gives rise to the digestive tract, liver, and pancreas?
questions.explanation: The slide lists the digestive tract, liver, and pancreas as endoderm derivatives.

questions.q: Which germ layer gives rise to bone, kidney, and the circulatory system?
questions.explanation: Bone, kidney, and circulatory and lymphatic systems are listed as mesoderm derivatives.

questions.q: In what year was the Till and McCulloch experiment shown performed?
questions.explanation: The slide title identifies the Till and McCulloch experiment as occurring in 1961.

questions.q: How were bone-marrow cells delivered to the irradiated mice?
questions.explanation: The experimental diagram specifies intravenous injection of bone-marrow cells.

questions.q: Which term means that a stem cell can produce more stem cells like itself?
questions.explanation: Self-renewal is the ability to generate additional stem cells.

questions.q: What metabolic and proliferative state is associated with many tissue stem cells?
options: Terminally differentiated with no renewal capacity
questions.explanation: The slide describes stem cells as capable of quiescence, with no division and low metabolic activity.

questions.q: Which two scientists shared the 2012 Nobel Prize highlighted on the slide?
questions.explanation: John Gurdon and Shinya Yamanaka shared the 2012 prize for discoveries concerning cellular reprogramming.

questions.q: From which differentiated tissue were Gurdon's donor nuclei obtained?
questions.explanation: The donor nuclei came from intestinal epithelial cells of feeding tadpoles.

questions.q: What fraction of differentiated-cell nuclear transplants produced normal tadpoles on the slide?
questions.explanation: The slide reports 10 normal tadpoles from 726 transplants, approximately 1.5%.

questions.q: What differentiated starting cell type was used in Yamanaka's experiment shown here?
questions.explanation: The source cells shown are mouse embryonic fibroblasts.

questions.q: How many candidate genes were initially screened using retroviral delivery?
questions.explanation: The slide states that 24 candidate genes were initially used to search for reprogramming factors.

questions.q: What assay readout was used to judge successful reprogramming combinations?
questions.explanation: The graphs compare colony number after testing different factor combinations.

questions.q: What general strategy narrowed the original candidate set to four factors?
options: Systematic factor removal and reduced combinations
questions.explanation: Factors were removed and smaller combinations tested to identify those required for colony formation.

questions.q: What does a normal karyotype establish about candidate iPSCs?
options: They have grossly normal chromosome number and structure
They can form every germ layer
They are free of all point mutations
questions.explanation: Karyotyping checks chromosome number and major structural integrity.

questions.q: Why is teratoma formation used alongside karyotyping?
options: It tests multilineage differentiation rather than chromosome integrity
It proves the absence of all tumors
questions.explanation: The two assays answer different questions: karyotype checks chromosomes, while teratoma tissues demonstrate broad differentiation.

questions.q: Which technology is proposed for correcting disease-causing mutations in patient-derived iPSCs?
questions.explanation: The slide proposes combining iPSCs with CRISPR/Cas9 for gene correction.

questions.q: What enables drug screening directly on a disease-relevant target cell type?
questions.explanation: Patient iPSCs can be directed into the relevant cell type and used for large-scale drug screening.

questions.q: How were Rx-positive cells visualized in the optic-cup culture?
questions.explanation: Rx-positive cells appear GFP-positive in the culture.

questions.q: Which matrix proteins are named as an alternative to Matrigel in the culture conditions?
questions.explanation: The slide names laminin plus entactin as matrix proteins used in the low-serum culture.

questions.q: Which fluorescent marker identifies the developing vesicles in the time-course images?
questions.explanation: The green signal is labeled Rx-GFP and marks retinal-field identity.

questions.q: Which region of the spherical vesicle invaginates to form neural-retina tissue?
questions.explanation: The distal portion invaginates and expresses neural-retina markers.

questions.q: Which marker pair supports retinal pigment epithelium identity in the outer epithelium?
questions.explanation: The outer epithelium expresses RPE-associated markers including Mitf and Otx2.

questions.q: Which organ is specifically important for T-cell maturation?
questions.explanation: T-cell precursors mature in the thymus.
